utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters. Is everybody ready? Thank you. Today in the courtroom we have Mr. Niko Lukin. I believe that is the case; is that correct? Good morning, sir. Can you hear me? You will read the solemn declaration that will be proffered to you by the usher. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. For the moment, you will be answering the questions posed to you by Mr. Mikulicic who is present here. Go ahead, please. Mr. Mikulicic, the floor is yours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, colleagues. Good morning, Mr. Lukin. I am attorney Mikulicic, I represent Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski together with my colleague, Mr. Joka. I am going to pose you some questions and I would like you to answer them to the best of your knowledge. Are you comfortable, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I was born on 26 January, 1932.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, what is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you religious?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your religion, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, where do you live?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I live in the village of Hrasno -- sorry, I was born in the village of Hrasno, and I live in the village of Cetovic (phoen) in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spent all your life in the area of the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, my entire life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I went to the elementary school in the Busovaca municipality, and I continued with my training in Zenica where I also completed my work career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, what kind of training did you get in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: When I first started working at Zenica steel mill, I was first working at a lower-ranking job, and then through my career, I kept receiving training, so I passed the first stage and I became highly qualified worker and then I later became a foreman and I became a shift chief, and that is the job which I was at on my retirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: It was the steel mill at Zenica. It was a huge steel mill works employing about 23.000 workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you retire, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I retired in early 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, what is the state of your health?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I have to say that during the war, I had some troubles. My heart is not quite well, my blood pressure is unstable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have certain troubles with your heart?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you receiving any medication?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. I do receive some medication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did do my military service in the JNA for two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was two years. Do you recall where it was and when it was?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I served in Macedonia between 1952 and 1954.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your compulsory military service, did you receive any military rank?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. After I finished with my military service, I took a job, I worked for 40 years, and then I retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing your military service, were you a member of any reserve?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, you said that you spent all your life in the Busovaca area, so I would imagine that you know this area quite well?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I was born there and I spent all my life there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, do you recall early 1993 when, in the Busovaca area, in your hometown, a conflict broke out between the Muslims and the Croats. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when these conflicts started? What was the event that marked the beginning of the conflict in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I could not recall the exact date, but I believe it was in early February, somewhere around there, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Bad things happened between ethnic groups. Muslims and Croats came into conflict, and a lot of innocent people suffered. In fact, it was only the innocent people who really came to harm at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, during those events, what was your role? What did you do at that time? You already told us that you were retired, but did you become involved in these events?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: In 1993, maybe in early March, a home guard detachment was established, and we believed -- we who were retired, we thought that we should get involved, so we became home guards and we were involved in providing security for certain facilities, such as health centres, schools, and such. And then later on, as there were not enough fighters and there were not regular soldiers in the prison -- I don't know how to call that facility -- then we were assigned to those duties, to guard those people. So for a while, I worked there, and during that period, I had an incident, I sustained a head injury, and after this injury, I took a sick leave. I spent several months on this sick leave, and at the end of this sick leave period, I was reassigned to the prison. I had nothing to do with the people there, but I was assigned to a gate through which I would let in vehicles and people who had permits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Lukin, let's go back to early March 1993 when you became involved in the home guard or Domobran company in Busovaca. Were you issued a uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. The home guards or Domobrans who were there were not issued any uniforms. We were wearing our civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about weapons? Were you issued any weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, we were given some weapons. It could have been -- it could have been weapons from World War I. It was old rifles, M-48, so it was very old weapons and we didn't even get any ammunition for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, our conversation is being interpreted into English and French, so I would like to ask you to please talk a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Oh, you mean more slowly? No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, you told us that you were a part of the Domobran company, that you were not issued any uniform, that you were issued some old weapons for which you never had any ammunition, and that you were assigned to secure certain facilities.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: That's right, certain facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, were you also assigned to Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. I was assigned to the Kaonik facility, but it was only one building that we were assigned to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, where exactly is your home?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: My home is about 500 metres away from the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in a matter of speaking, we can say that you are the first neighbour to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: That is correct. It is 500 metres away and I could see from my house the gate through which people came in and out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given that you lived there even before the conflict, can you recall who was using this facility before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, it was the army, it was the JNA which used it, and then in 1991, the army pulled out, and the facility remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, do you happen to know what was the use of these facilities in Kaonik which was used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. These facilities were full of ammunition, projectiles, and all kinds of weapons, and when the war started, this army -- how shall I call it? -- the JNA, they took everything away that they wanted and the facilities remained somewhat empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we could say that this was a depot?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, you could call them a depot or warehouses, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first came on duty to Kaonik as a member of the Domobran company for securing the facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. I first came there on 15 April, 1993. That's when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- did you say it was in April, because you said that you were mobilised in March.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, mid-April. On that same month, on 25th April, 1993, that's when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, what exactly was your duty there? What were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Our task of these Domobrans was to provide security for this facility to be of service to these people, to help them go to the toilet, to provide water, heating, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your duty to secure the facility from the outside or were you supposed to be inside?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. We were not supposed to go in at all. We were just on the outside to make sure that nobody would approach it or do something there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were people in there. Who were these people there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Those were people from the neighbouring villages, villagers, and they were kept there for their own safety, and they were there for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, you mentioned that these were villagers from the surrounding villages. Can you recall which villages these were from which these people were kept there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Of course. These were my neighbours, so to speak. They were villages of Skradno, Loncari, and Strane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, do you recall whether, in the immediate vicinity of these villages, there was any fighting, any armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: From the areas from which these people came, and they came there for their own security, that's exactly where the fighting took place, in these villages where these -- from where these people were brought and where they were kept for their own security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, how were these people accommodated? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, they were accommodated in a building there. It used to be a military building, and then they were put up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were there day and night; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what were their conditions there, where did they sleep? Did they have any blankets, did they have any stoves?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: They did have blankets. That was provided. Mr. Warden saw to it and then later on some stoves were also put in there so that these premises could be heated. You can't say that the conditions were very good, but it was a wartime situation, so that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, what were the hygienic conditions for these people? Where did they go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: The toilet was near this building. There was only a short path that separated it from there, and that's where they went to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they able to go to the toilet when they needed to or were there any restrictions there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: There were no restrictions there. As far as that is concerned, we did everything to accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they receive water from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You see, there was a water installation there which we used to -- which we used as well, and so they shared that facility with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was municipal water?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the surrounding villages used this waterworks as well as Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: That is correct. The schools, villages, and also the facility where these people were kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, do you recall whether throughout this period of conflict the supply of water was steady or were there any interruptions?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were some interruptions because it was an old installation and so there were some breakdowns, so -- but if the breakdowns happened, then they would be repaired, and the supply would be reinstalled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the food that these civilians were receiving?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: The food was being brought there and we all ate it. Those people who were kept there as well as those people who guarded them shared the food, and the food as such, sometimes it was better, sometimes it was not so good. There were wartime conditions, so sometimes we didn't have enough food stocks to provide good food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many meals were given every day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: There were three meals being given every day. After a while, the supplies of food diminished, so we switched to two meals a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the guards, did they also switch to two meals a day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the supply of food and other goods, like fuel, in the Busovaca area at that time? Was it regular or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You couldn't call it regular at all. The whole area was blocked off for almost six months, so you couldn't reach the area on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Lukin, you said that it was blocked. Do you mean Busovaca was?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the town of Busovaca or the wider area?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: It was a wider area. It also included Vitez and it included the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true then that the population of this area was surrounded and that the communications between Busovaca and the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were cut off?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: The only communication line that was not cut off was Vitez-Busovaca -- between Vitez and Busovaca, but the entire area of Vitez and Busovaca was cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, you lived all your life in the Busovaca area, and you know this area very well. You probably know the configuration of the terrain there as well. Can you tell me, during these wartime events, was there any location, any spot in the Busovaca area, where there was no fighting, where there was no shooting, and there was no shelling?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. Everything in the Busovaca area, all points within the Busovaca area, were within the shooting range, so every village, every spot in the area, was within firing range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any shells -- did any shells ever fall on the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You could say that they fell everywhere, that they were falling at all places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about around your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Of course. And as I said, we were very close to the prison, and a lot of shells fell there, maybe the most. A number of houses were actually damaged. However, luckily, nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were killed and injured people in the town of Busovaca and in the other surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was the first defensive lines away from the town of Busovaca and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: They were maybe one to 1.5 kilometres away at the most, so that these lines were very close of this area of Busovaca and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this situation was similar in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, when you came to serve your duty at the Kaonik facility, did you meet Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet him often or just once or twice?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Several times. Because I only spent a short time there, so we only met several times. When we arrived as Domobrans, he held a meeting with us, and in this meeting he advised us that we should treat these people decently and fairly, that these people were there on a temporary basis, and while they were there, that they should be treated as well and correct as possible, and even without that, these people were our colleagues from work, we travelled, worked with them for 20 and more years, some of them actually worked in my department, and so we tried to help them while they were in this facility. To some of them, we even brought food, we would bring them cigarettes since they were our colleagues from work, and I thought that this would be part of our conscience and we also felt that this was our duty on a humane basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Speaking of Mr. Aleksovski, would you recognise him if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Of course, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise him here in this room?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you see him? Where is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski is sitting over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness showed in the direction of the accused and identified him as Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, do you recall when you first saw Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski and when you saw him the next several times, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I saw him wearing civilian clothes several times and several times wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a uniform was it; can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: It was some kind of a camouflage uniform without any insignia. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any rank or any other insignia?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. No insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you came to provide security for this facility, Mr. Aleksovski pointed out to you that with respect to the civilians which you came to guard at this facility, that you should treat them fairly and humanely?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow those instructions?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Of course. Because it would have been a shame to behave in any other way. As I said, we commuted together for a period of years, we worked together, so it would have been both brutal and inhumane to behave in any other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, did you personally see or hear that these people were mistreated, that these people were beaten, or somebody would inflict any injuries to them?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: While I was there, no such incidents occurred and nothing of that kind happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, did these people have enough food? Did they have such conditions that in the given wartime circumstances, they could function normally?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Listen. Given that it was wartime, you couldn't describe the conditions as normal. I'm not sure, though, that they could have been provided with better conditions than there were at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you know the Busovaca area. Do you know whether there is another similar facility in the Busovaca area, similar to Kaonik, where these people could have been accommodated?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. There was a facility in Draga, but I don't think that these people could have been accommodated there as well as in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, do you know how these people found themselves in Kaonik? In other words, who brought them there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I was not present when these people were brought there. I just found them there. Who brought them there and how, that, I could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that, according to you, since these people came from the surrounding villages where the fighting had taken place, that they were put up there for their own security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because it was the safest place for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, did you see or hear that people from these surrounding villages would come to Kaonik themselves in order to feel safe there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: There were cases where people would come there because they felt safe there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of the people who came on their own free will there, to stay there? Do you know any names?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, I could not tell you any names, but I know that there were such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know from which village?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: From the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, while working there at Kaonik providing security, did you see any people who were there, that they became ill in any way, any kind of health problems, skin problems, or any kind of disease?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: There were no such cases where people needed any medical attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, can you tell us whether the Kaonik facility itself was sometimes under fire, that is, shelled?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did it ever happen that either civilians or anyone who was there at that time was injured from any of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether any of the guards were injured? You said that you yourself were injured.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were four of us among guards who were injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were four. How were you injured and where did it happen?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: This happened immediately next to the facility where we were on duty. We were right there in order to provide security, and it was evening, it was probably about 8.00 p.m., and we were nearby, and a shell fell on a tree and then I sustained a head injury, and a colleague of mine was injured -- had his genitals injured, and the others were injured in other parts of their body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after your injuries?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: When we were injured, Mr. Aleksovski put us in a car and drove us to the health centre in order to give us medical attention. There, at the health centre, they did what they could, and then what they couldn't, because they couldn't do everything, they took us to the Bila hospital and there they treated us and then released us to our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is how you finished with your duty in providing security at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Exactly in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, can you tell us, while you were in Kaonik, whether people, these civilians from the surrounding villages, that these people were taken out of Kaonik in order to provide some kind of labour?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. The people who were there were occasionally taken out to perform some tasks. I believe it was trench-digging or something like that. And there were other people who were taken to dig these trenches and dugouts, whatever you call them. Also my brother was taken there, and there were some people of Orthodox religion who were taken there. So whenever there was a need to do such a thing, everybody was taken there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you mentioned people from the area. Now, when you say that, are you referring to the HVO personnel as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they would come and ask that people be taken. So if I understand you correctly, they would come to Kaonik, they would ask for a certain number of people, they would take them out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, did you notice, when these people would come back to Kaonik, that they were injured or did you see on them traces of any injuries or any disease or anything?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, I saw no such person. I saw them coming back tired but not injured or sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, you mentioned that this labour duty, digging or whatever, other kind of work, was not the sole duty of the people who were there but also people who were outside and who were not involved in the defence.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: As I said, my brother who is retired, also went on that duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old is your brother?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: He's two years younger than I am. He was born in 1935, so he is now 63.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about your son?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: He's young. He was born in 1958, he fell ill, he was not able to go to the defence line, so he had work duty and he went to dig on a daily basis. Not only my son, but there were others who did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, how was this organised? Would somebody come for your brother and your son to go out to this work duty?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, the military police would come and they would take those people there, wherever the work was needed, and after that, they would return them home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to your brother and your son on which locations they performed those work duties? Where did they dig?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to them. They dug at Strane, Podyele, they dug up at the Kula region. They were several places and they worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Strane, Kula, Podyele. Were these places near the defence line or were these places away from the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Wherever these people worked, that was always close to these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they had to work there? What did they do there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I don't think we understood each other. Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to your brother and your son.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: The military needed these lines fortified so that they would not fall, so that the people down in Kaonik and Busovaca would not be threatened. In other words, in short, that these lines would not fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Do you know, Mr. Lukin, whether your brother or your son, on those occasions, would see or whether they told you that some people were injured, killed, or similar during the labour duty?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I talked to them, but to my knowledge and as far as they told me, they saw no such incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Lukin, whether during the labour duty, whether these people, for instance, your son and your brother and others, whether they received food?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, if they were taken out by night, they did not receive any food at night, but they would receive food in the morning, so that they would be able to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it was necessary to go during the night?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you know, the lines were targeted, and it could be then seen during the day that people were digging and were in greater danger, and that is why it was decided to do the work duty during the night, in order to reduce the danger to the people who were involved in the digging of trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Lukin, you now live at home, you are retired.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any connection with the Domobran company in which you served? Does it still exist?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, it has been dissolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any connections with any other military unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Lukin. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you have the floor. Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukin.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukin, I think that the Domobran unit was not actually part of the HVO itself, it was part of the municipal defence forces and, as such, came under the authority of the mayor; is that right, of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I would not agree with you because the Domobran regiment was not part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there may have been -- you may have misunderstood me. That was the point I was making. Domobran wasn't part of the HVO, it was part of the -- it came under the authority of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was part of the municipal forces, under the mayor of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the mayor would have to do with that. Well, it was the commander of the regiment who was in charge, and the mayor, to my knowledge, had nothing to do with the Domobran regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what part of the government, if I can call it that, of the regional government, did it report to? It must have been part of some structure, surely. It can't have just went to the commander and stopped there.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, I know that they had their own commander or the person in charge, and that there was somebody else who was in charge, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us this: When you joined the Domobran unit, did you go to the local municipal building in Busovaca or how was it that you became part of it? How did you manage to join up in the Domobran?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: In order to join the Domobrans, we were invited one day, all of us who were expected to contribute, in case the security was threatened, the security of the people, and it was then decided so, and we were then deployed to serve in the way that I have already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell me, who invited you and where did you go when you received the invitation?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: When I was invited, I went to a local school where we received our tasks to secure the facilities and the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you went to the local school, who addressed you? Who spoke to you there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: When I went to the school, I talked to our commander who was in charge of the Domobrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive notice to go to the school by some written form of notice?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I received a written notice, not only myself, but all the others, and we were invited to come and be deployed where the need arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the written piece of paper that you received, did it have any stamps or markers or it to indicate where it had come from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, there was a seal, but I did not attach any importance to it, what kind of a seal or a stamp it was and what was written on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it it wasn't the seal of the HVO. That you seem sure of.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't have been the HVO because it was a separate role of the Domobran regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, did you know a guard that had the name, I think it's a nickname of Pisar, P-I-S-A-R?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, I don't know any person by that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the Kaonik facility, to the prison, it was your duty, was it not, to prevent people from coming into the prison as well as to prevent people from escaping from the prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you could say so, to prevent people from entering and from getting out in order to prevent them from being harassed or exposed to any danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, were you successful in keeping people in the prison; in other words, did anyone escape from the prison when you were there, at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, nobody escaped, but I can also tell you that I was there for a short time, just ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, we can only talk about that time. And during the same period of time, were you successful in keeping people out who were not wanted or who weren't permitted to go into the prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, there was no need to prevent anyone because there were no attempts of such kind, that somebody would reach those people and do them any harm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that the -- it wasn't terribly difficult or it mustn't have been thought to have been terribly difficult to keep people out or to keep people in, if necessary, because you had an old weapon and no ammunition which wouldn't have been very effective, I take it, if you had come to a confrontation?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: The weapons should not have been there as far as the fear was concerned that somebody could harm them, but there was -- I mean, the threat or coming to any danger was not at question at all. No such situation could have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you know, there was no threat to the prisoners from the outside, at least during the period of time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, no, no such threat existed as far as those people were concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of having a system, I think, of permits for people to come into the prison. Can you tell me about that? What were these permits? Were they in written form?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, they were not in written forms, but people would come of their own free volition because they believed it was the securest place for them to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about civilians, I'm not talking about Muslim civilian people, I'm talking about other people that would come to the gate in order to come into the prison. I think you said in your evidence that they would have permits.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was when I was not in charge of security but when I was at the gate, then people would arrive with some sort of permits, and on the basis of those permits and the permit (sic) that was given of the head foreman of the shift, we could allow them to get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the permit was issued by somebody in the prison itself?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, no. People would come from the outside; for instance, the Red Cross people, they would come to the gate and then consult with the people at the gate, and with the approval of the warden, of his assistants, and they were allowed to go and visit the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't always in written form, it was sometimes the warden saying, "Yes, that person can come in"?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, if they were already there, I mean, if they worked there regularly, they didn't need written permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking of people who weren't regular guards in the prison, I'm talking of people who weren't regular guards. In those cases, are you saying to me that the permit for them to enter was a written document that was signed by Mr. Aleksovski, or was it sometimes a case of him simply saying, "Yes, those persons can come in"?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, they would talk over the telephone, and after his -- after the approval, the person would be let in to enter the facility up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was it always Mr. Aleksovski who had to give approval, or was there somebody else authorised to approve a person's entry into the facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you know, sometimes Mr. Aleksovski would not be there, he had his aides, and the persons who were in charge of shifts, shift leaders, and they would give oral approval that someone should be let in up in the prison area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember ever an occasion happening when Mr. Aleksovski said to you, "No, that person is not to come in?" Do you ever remember that happening at all at any stage that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, I don't remember anything like that happening, and there were no such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, though, however, if Mr. Aleksovski had said to you, "No, that person's not to come in," you would have then refused entry for that person to come through. That would have been part of your job.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, yes. It would be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you said that you first came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I said that I arrived there to the camp on the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said in your evidence that sometime after you arrived, that the stoves were installed in order for the people to keep warm. Do you know how long after it was that you arrived that these stoves were installed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: When I arrived there, the stoves were already there. They were already installed in the facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see them actually installed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, because when I got there, they were already there. They were already installed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of Muslim civilian prisoners going to use the toilet facilities. I take it these were the Muslim civilian prisoners who were in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would guard them as they would use the toilet, I take it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, we were beside them while they were completing their -- while they were going to the WC, we would be there, and then they would be returned to the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you actually escorted them to the toilet and back again, you would be armed, you'd have whatever arms that you had, even though you might not have had any ammunition --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, we had some arms that I already mentioned, you know, the arms from World War I and that we had no ammunition for those arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get any ammunition for these arms?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: After some time, we did receive a few bullets, but it was a very, very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some questions about the villages surrounding the area of Kaonik that you know about anyway. I take it that in those sort of villages that surround the Kaonik facility, they're not all supplied with running water through a main system of water, are they? I take it a lot of the villages have wells.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, some did not. It is true. For instance, the village of Skradno had water supply while Strane and Loncari were not part of the municipal water supply system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those cases they would have had either a village well or a well attached to the houses, the individual houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you know, the people who were there, they took water from the same water supply system that we had, the people who lived there, and they used the same water, the people who were accommodated in these facilities. But people who lived up there in the villages, they had their own wells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, people who lived near the Lasva River would have had access to those water purposes as well, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You know, the Lasva River, the water there is not potable, so you can use it to wash your clothes and things like that, but not to drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also in these villages, people would have had animals, like cows and chicks and hens and things of that nature, that would be very typical in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they would have had orchards --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you know, people from those villages had livestock, they had cows and sheep and hens, and all sorts of livestock, and we, as neighbours, did take care about their livestock while they were away, and there were many such instances, and I was one of those who took care about the livestock of one of my neighbours until the situation normalised, when the armed conflict stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this neighbour who you looked after the livestock for was a Muslim neighbour?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it also that people in these villages surrounding this area had little vegetable gardens as well which they would plant food in?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet I think you spoke in your evidence about there being a time when there was a great shortage of food.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, there was a time with great shortages of food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was a shortage of food in the Kaonik prison and with the army and feeding the soldiers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, no, nobody had at that time, and the people who were accommodated there, the army and anybody else, because we all had small rations because the area was blocked and it was impossible to ensure food supplies that would be sufficient to feed the civilians, the army, and the rest of the people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you went home to your house, which I understand was nearby, you would have had livestock and --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you would have had a vegetable garden?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you may not have been able to get all of the food you wanted, but you had, I take it, sufficient food at your home?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, at one time, yes, but there was a time when that was not true because there was a time of shortage, and I did take some food from my own family supplies to bring it to someone -- some food to my friends, if I may call them so, and we shared the little food that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, you had sufficient food at home to be able to actually bring food to the prison because of the official government supply of food was in short supply?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, I said that we did not have enough food and nobody else had, for that matter. But as far as the humane relationship is concerned, people realised that those who had food should bring it to those who hadn't, so that's how we shared the little food that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that didn't have it were the people in the prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, all of us did not have enough food. I said so. And while we were in prison, everybody had the same rations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these good people that were in prison, these Muslim neighbours of yours, they weren't there because they were vicious criminals or anything of that nature, were they? They were good people.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you could say so, yes, but because of the circumstances, the people had to be brought there for their own security and for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't come there voluntarily, though. You know that, don't you? It's not as though the whole lot of them just --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know. I can't tell you because I said that I came later when they were already there. Whether they came there of their own free will or whether they were brought there, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would it surprise you if I told you that there's been evidence in these proceedings that these people were brought there by the military police under force?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that so I cannot talk to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that the Croatian people in these surrounding villages, they stayed in their villages, did they, during the course of the war, those who weren't engaged in fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Some villagers did and some villagers did not, and there were Croats who were expelled from certain villages too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand that. The Croats that were expelled from certain villages, they went as refugees to other Croatian villages, did they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: They went to different places. If they had an opportunity, they would even leave the territory of their municipality. They went -- they also went to certain places from which the Muslims had left. They went to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that a lot of the Muslim people that weren't sort of trapped by the war, if I can call it that, they left too and went to places like Zenica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: There were such cases too and there were those who stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they stayed in their villages until such time as -- well, you may not know this -- until such time as they were rounded up and brought into the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was no such roundup by the HVO military police of the Croatian civilians, were they? They weren't rounded up and put into Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Those who broke some laws or violated some laws were brought there, and they would be brought to this Kaonik facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were people who had committed criminal offences, but we've already established that your Muslim neighbours were not criminals.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, you could not call them criminals. Nobody said that they were criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the fact that you had a meeting early on with Mr. Aleksovski, and he told you to treat the Muslim civilian --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- prisoners fairly and properly. This was an order he gave to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Whether this was an order or something done on a humane basis, I don't know, but we felt that it would be humane to treat these people in such a way because, as I said, we worked, commuted with these people for years. They were our colleagues from work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might clarify that for me because I'm a little uncertain about it. This issue about the humane treatment of the prisoners, was that something imposed upon you by Mr. Aleksovski by way of an order, or was it something you merely chose to do yourself because you knew that these people were innocent civilians, or was it perhaps a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You see, what Mr. Aleksovski said was nothing bad. He said that these people should be treated as well as possible. But even if we were not advised by him in this way, we treated them in a humane and collegiate way, so to speak, because we worked with them for years and it is by no means that we treated them badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you viewed them to be good, honest people and there was no reason whatsoever for treating them --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Of course, there was no reason for any kind of mistreatment. There was absolutely no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen, do you think, what would Mr. Aleksovski do if you had mistreated these people? What would he have done to you if you had mistreated these people?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: He would mete out some punishment for any infractions like that, maybe even some more severe punishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that, so far as you're concerned, you took the view that he wouldn't tolerate any breaches of discipline?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: If we were to do -- if we did something bad, he definitely would start some kind of proceedings against us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, and I'm talking about the first half of 1993 in particular, it was not permissible, was it, for ordinary civilian people who were in no way connected with the military to wear military clothes?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I did not understand you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying is that you were not permitted, were you, to wear military-type clothes, either wholly or partly, during that period of time because the only people who were permitted to wear military-type clothes were those persons who were in some way connected with the military.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: We were not allowed to wear any type of uniform, so we were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that only people who had some sort of connection to the military were permitted to wear military clothes? It was illegal to wear military clothes if you weren't in some way connected to the military?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I did not understand that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me take it perhaps in a few more steps. There was a shortage of military uniforms during that period in 1993, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the government was anxious to ensure that only those people who were working for the military would receive military uniforms which were in short supply?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so unless people were actually connected with the military, whether it be the HVO or some other unit, they were not permitted to wear military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No," they weren't permitted -- is that what you're saying? They weren't permitted to?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: It was not permitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said in answer to one of the questions by Mr. Mikulicic that there were no cases where people needed medical attention. I take it from that you're not suggesting there was no cases whatsoever, there's just none that you are aware of; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I was only speaking of the period when I was there, that there were no such cases that anybody needed any medical attention or care during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the Muslim civilian prisoners were taken out for trench-digging, were they tied up? Were they restrained, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, I could see, but those people were not tied up. They would just board the trucks and were taken to locations where some work needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the Muslim civilian prisoners being tied up before they were taken out of the camp? Did you ever see that happen when you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people that took these Muslim civilian prisoners out for trench-digging, they were -- what? -- military police, were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these military police were in uniform and they were armed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the military police had to take precautions to ensure that these people wouldn't escape, these Muslim civilian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, of course, because they were also charged with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when your brother went trench-digging and your son went trench-digging, he wasn't sent there as a prisoner, was he? He was someone who was co-opted to assist with the war movement?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't really of their own free will that they went there, but such needs arose and the military police would come and take them there, and after they were done, they would bring them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were citizens of the municipality who were being called upon --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- by the government to assist with the war effort?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: War effort? I'm not sure that I understood who was called to help in the war effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take it more slowly. When it came to your brother and your son being taken to dig trenches, their assistance was sought --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- by the military police because there was a shortage of manpower and in order to protect the municipality --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- their assistance was required?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They weren't arrested and taken -- what didn't happen to your brother and son was they were not --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- they were not confined in a prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they went out to dig trenches, they didn't have armed guards there who would shoot them in the back if they tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, the military police was with them as it was with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, excuse me for interrupting you, but maybe it would be good if we took a break so that we can all take a little rest. So we will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, please continue. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, how old was your son when he was taken trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: He was 38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your brother, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: My brother at that time was 63.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just going back for a little moment to the Domobran unit that you spoke of retired people being in that. Was there also young men in it as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You mean among the Domobrans?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. For the most part these were people advanced in age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that your brother and son had said to you that they knew of no one who had been injured at the front when they were trench-digging. Other than from them telling you, did you hear from other source where the people had been injured or killed when they were taken out for trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, I did not hear that there were any injured during that labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the military police would come to take the Muslim civilian prisoners out for the purposes of trench-digging, they would come in the morning, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases when they would come in the morning or in the evening, depending on when certain works were needed out in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people were selected, the Muslim civilian prisoners were selected according to a list?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand how -- what you mean by according to the list. Let's say the people were chosen from a list if any work needed to be done, some younger people were usually selected, and those who were not well, they were sort of exempt. They were spared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Aleksovski was there, wasn't he, from time to time when people were being selected and taken out for trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Sometimes he was not there. There were times when Mr. Aleksovski was not there. He had his own work hours and maybe somebody else whose shift it was would assume the role of Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I am not disputing that there were times when he wasn't there I am just saying that there were also times when he was there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, there were times when he was there, and when he was there he was sort of controlling us there and he would observe whether we carry out our duties properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did you know that these people were going for trench-digging? Did the HVO police tell you that, did they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: We knew, because the -- a door -- the gate would open, the people would board a vehicle. You didn't need to know more than that. You would see that people were leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But it's known that they are actually going to be used for trench-digging, was the point I was aiming at. Did the HVO military police say, for example, we need "X" number of people for the purposes of digging trenches? Did they tell you that so that you knew that was what was happening? Or did Mr. Aleksovski tell you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: You see, we who were there securing the facility had no idea whether they would go or not. We would just see when the police arrived, when the gate would open, the vehicle would be brought in. But if -- we didn't know that in advance as Domobrans. We were not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you yourself don't know whether or not the Muslim civilian prisoners that were taken trench-digging were beaten or not, but you couldn't know that because you weren't at the trenches, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose your son or your brother never complained of being beaten when they were trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, they did not complain. They did not say anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know during this period of time that some of the Muslim civilian prisoners were taken out for the purposes of being used as human shields for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that. I do not know that anything of that kind happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, I take it, your son or your brother were never used as HVO human shields?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I assumed that they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think they would have told you if they had of been, wouldn't they? It's something that they would likely tell you about?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, probably they would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, can you tell us, approximately, how many people were in the hangar? How many Muslim civilian prisoners were in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: We did not have access to that information, and we did not know the number of people who were in the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to have a rough idea. I know you obviously didn't sit down and count them, but was there -- did it appear to you that there were more than a hundred or less than a thousand? Are you able to give us any estimate at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to give any figure. I never entered the facility, had no access to that, so I would not be able to give you any number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of people -- I'll withdraw that, Your Honours. I take it, that you are aware that in some of the villages surrounding the Kaonik facility, that some of those villages were destroyed and a lot of the people -- a lot of the people were killed. You knew that that happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I don't know that they were killed, but since I lived right next door to it, I did see that on some occasions some buildings were on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you lived fairly closely to the village of Ahmici, didn't you? That was fairly close to where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No, not very near the Ahmici village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Something like seven kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew it had been -- you knew it had been razed to the ground and that there was allegations about a lot of people being killed there, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, objection regarding the village of Ahmici, because the village of Ahmici has absolutely not related to the charges in this indictment before this Trial Chamber. And with respect to the decision of the Trial Chamber of 19 June '98, where it states that the Prosecution needs to limit itself to the charges set out in the indictment, that is the basis for our objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be demonstrating the significance of this line of cross-examination as it emerges. And it will touch upon matters which were discussed in evidence in chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can you tell us in advance what is the importance of this question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I certainly could, Your Honours, but I would ask that the witness be requested to remove his headset, if that's the case. Yes, Your Honours, the line of questioning is that there's been suggestion raised by this and other witnesses that have come here that a lot of the -- well, not a lot, but a number of the people, the Muslim people, came to the Kaonik facility voluntarily. And the questions I am asking relate to the fact that there were places, such as Ahmici and others which were notorious places where people were killed, Muslim villages were -- things happened, like the buildings were burnt down, people were shot by the HVO, such that it may be that a number of these people that came to these areas, such as Kaonik, to seek protection and shelter, because they in fact wanted to get away from the attacks by the HVO. So that it's not a case of people being concerned about attacks from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they wanted to escape from, that they wanted to go to Kaonik because they felt it may have been safer than staying in their homes in a village like Ahmici where the evidence shows -- where there was notorious events that occurred. So it's that line of questioning. It comes to that conclusion. And I have -- I believe that this witness would know about what happened at Ahmici. I believe he would know that. He can say one way or the other. But that's where the line of questioning goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, what would you like to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to say -- to raise two points. The Defence absolutely respect the position of the Prosecution, but before that the Defence would like to clarify some points, if the Prosecution would like to pose a question along these lines. I think that first of all he would have to ask the witness whether the people were Ahmici were brought to Kaonik. And then if the answer is yes, then we see a relation. If the answer is no, we see no relation between this and our witness. So the Defence believes that the questioning should go along these lines. This is, perhaps, just a suggestion for the further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I think that Mr. Mikulicic is right, as far as the way of questioning is concerned. So you say that the question was that you want to know whether there were people from -- who were brought there, given the circumstances. Can you -- have you understood me, because you can only proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not prepared to proceed in the way that Mr. Mikulicic is saying I have to proceed, but I am prepared to change my line of questioning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I had no translation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You can resume your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, are you aware that during this period of time, that's in 1993 and the early part of 1993 through the whole of that period, that a number of villages in relatively close proximity to yourself were destroyed, and both Croat villages and Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, there were cases that people were killed from these villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the villages that were destroyed, the Croat villages, for example, were likely to have been destroyed by forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the villages that --

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- were predominantly Muslim were likely to have been destroyed by the forces of the HVO; that's the nature of war, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when people -- so when Muslim civilian citizens from the neighbourhood came to the Kaonik facility, you would agree with me, would you not, that more than likely they were in fear of being attacked by HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the war, and when the Kaonik facility was a JNA base, it was an ammunition dump, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wouldn't be able to say one way or the other, I take it, whether the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina still believed it to be an ammunition dump or a prison facility in which Muslims were being kept in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, they wouldn't believe that it was an ammunition depot or dump, because they knew when these facilities were evacuated and when all the mighty potential and arms and weapons were withdrew from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that something that you know? How do you know that? Tell me, how is it that you know that, that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have known that for sure, that it had been disbanded as an ammunition dump?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, they knew because the military facilities, such as they were in Kaonik, existed in Kacuni, and these facilities were vacated and evacuated simultaneously by the JNA troops, so which took with them everything that they needed. And it was evident, then, that the army knew what happened with the facility at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one final point is that when you were injured, you said that you were sent home in order to get better. Do you remember saying that, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. I even said the date when I was wounded, how long I was absent, and that I resumed my duty, but not in the prison, inside the prison, but outside at the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, that you would agree with me that it's common sense that it was considered that when you were injured and recovering, home would have been the best place for you to be, because it was warmer, it was safer, and there was a ready supply of water and food for you to help you in your recovery?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe just a few, Your Honours, if you allow me. Re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, can you tell us, according to your knowledge, from which villages in the Busovaca area people were brought or they arrived, civilian Muslims were brought or they arrived at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Loncari, the village of Strane and the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
