utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, were there any cases that, as far as the village of Ahmici was concerned, that some people would arrive or be brought to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Ahmici are in no way related to the -- to what happened in Kaonik and a facility at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Lukin, you also mentioned that some people, and by that I imply the population of Croat origin, that people who were not involved as fighters in the frontlines, and who were not involved in your Domobran company, in the same company in which you served, that those people would remain home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I did not understand you completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Lukin, that local population, and by that I imply local Croats, who were not engaged in the front or who were not serving in your Domobran company, is that true that they would remain home?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who remained home, did they have labour duty?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that apply -- did that apply to your son and your brother?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, what would happen if your son, or your brother, when military police would come to take them away for labour duty, what would happen if they refused?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, the same measures would be taken as against all others. Perhaps they would be punished or disciplined, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Lukin. Does Zlatko Aleksovski belong to your Domobran company?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zlatko Aleksovski have any powers as far as giving orders to Domobrans in the Domobran company were concerned?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did have such orders in your company?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: The commander of the Domobran company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness, a number of questions were put to you about the hygienic conditions in Kaonik Prison. Now, can you tell me how many toilets there were for all the inmates in that facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I don't suppose, then, you can answer the next question as to how many bathrooms there were in that facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: In that facility, the facility to be secured, the Domobrans, there were no bathrooms. But there were bathrooms in the neighbouring facility, and occasionally people would go there to take a bath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Lukin, I too have some questions for you. You said that you served at the entrance at the gate, and that you were there in order to allow people in, people in vehicles who had permits; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And you already said something about that when the Prosecutor asked you about the same thing. But I need some clarification there. We know that you were there, and that you spent only 10 days there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Who then -- who then would usually have those permits?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: For entering the grounds, permits were issued to people from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. But I said those who would be allowed to enter the grounds. Who would normally be given such permits?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, we who were on duty at the gate, we had a telephone, just for internal use, and when people would come to the gate who we -- whom we did not know, and who did not have the necessary documents, we would consult the shift leader or Mr. Zlatko whether or not we should allow them to enter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I understand that if there were people who would come without papers, that you would then seek permission or give them permission to enter, but people who already had permits with them, were they allowed to enter directly or did you have to consult Mr. Aleksovski in order to let them in?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, most frequently there was military police and they had those papers, and so there was no need for us to consult or to seek permission from Zlatko or from one of his assistants to allow such people to get in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lukin. But in addition to military police, there were other people, members of other organisations who already had such documents on them, such permits; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: I don't know that there were organisations who had such documents. I mentioned already military police and representatives of the Red Cross, and there were no other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And as far as the HVO soldiers were concerned, what about them? Did you understand me? Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, I have -- my question is as follows: HVO soldiers, did they have authorisation to enter or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: People who were employed in the prison, they had the permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. I see. But the HVO soldiers who did not work there, for instance, soldiers -- HVO soldiers who did not work in the prison, did they have or didn't they have to -- didn't they have such permits?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: They -- there were no such permits and they did not enter the prison grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, for instance, if a soldier, if an HVO soldier who was not employed in the prison, if such a person wanted to enter the prison grounds, you would have to consult Mr. Aleksovski about the permit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, but in most cases such persons would not arrive without documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. I have one more question for you, Mr. Lukin. You said that food was served three times a day or two times a day, and that in any case there were difficulties since you had food shortages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes, I said in the beginning we had enough food, but there were no shortages. And as the blockade continued, and it lasted for a long time, we had to distribute only two meals a day, or two rations a day. And I already said that it was the same food for all. People who were in the facility, people who served, and all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lukin. How was the food served? How was it served? Was it served in plates or in any other way?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: In the facility that we guarded, the food was distributed into rations and plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, then, individual rations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Did you -- were you aware of the fact that, or did you know, actually, how the civilians received their food, the civilian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: In the same way that was applied to all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. Another question. Did you know how a military police uniform looked like?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, they had the same uniform as the HVO soldiers, but the insignias were different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can you distinguish, or could you distinguish between the uniforms of a soldier and a military police, judging by the insignias they had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And the uniform that Mr. Aleksovski sometimes wore, was it the same as the uniform of the HVO or was it a uniform of the military police?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Well, it looked more like an HVO uniform, but without the insignia, and he frequently wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But if I understood you correctly, when he wore a military uniform, his uniform resembled more the uniform of the HVO than the uniform of a military police; did I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKO LUKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that the Trial Chamber has no further questions for you, Mr. Lukin. Thank you very much for coming here, and I hope that you will have a safe journey back to your home. Thank you very much, Mr. Lukin. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence now calls the witness by the name of Ivica Bagaric. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bagaric. Can you hear me? You will now read the solemn declaration that will be given to you by our official.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir. You can be seated, so as to feel comfortable. Do you feel comfortable, sir? For the time being you will answer the questions which will be posed to you by Mr. Mikulicic. You have the floor, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would just kindly ask, before we start with the questioning of Mr. Bagaric, if I can consult my client for a short time, for about 30 seconds to be more precise. Do I have your permission to consult my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You have the permission, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I am ready now to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Mikulicic and I represent Mr. Aleksovski, together with my colleague, Mr. Joka. I am going to ask you some questions and please be so kind to answer them to the best of your ability. Mr. Bagaric, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1942 in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend your childhood in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you reside in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak of Busovaca, are you talking about the town of Busovaca or the wider area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I live in the village, I guess, of Kaonik, but I went to school in the Kaonik town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in your own family house or in some apartment building?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: In my own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you religious?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: It's Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the elementary school in Busovaca and from the secondary school in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a secondary school in Zenica was it that --

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: It was a trade school and I was specialised in metals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take employment right after school?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you become employed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: In Zenica, in a company called Pappero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, after I graduated from the secondary school I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this, approximately?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: This was in 1962, '63.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you completed your military service in the former JNA, did you have any obligations with the reserves during the period of time of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have any duties, but occasionally, since I was a mechanic in the old artillery during my military service, so during some military exercises I went there for some repairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You continued to live in Kaonik in the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been at the same address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you retired or are you still employed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I am neither. I was wounded, so I received disability. But the company where I worked is -- is no longer in operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, do you recall the beginning of the conflict in Busovaca, when was this? And I am speaking now about the Muslim-Croat conflict of 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: This was early on. I could not give you the exact time, but it was early in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: There was so much shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes and then also I was mobilised until I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were mobilised and to what military unit you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised in early 1993 and the military unit was the HVO. That is an HVO unit, they were called the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Thereafter I was transferred to the Domobran unit, but I don't know what its name was, because I was considered a bit older. So I was assigned to the Domobrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were transferred from the HVO unit to the Domobran unit because of your age?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other persons who, like you, were members of the Domobran unit, were these also older people? What was the age group there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part they were old and they were even older than I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you joined the Domobran units, did you receive a uniform or some weapons from that unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I did not receive anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume that you had a uniform from before, when you were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I had it from there. But I did not receive anything from the Domobrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, does that mean that you were allowed to take the uniform, which was issued to you by the HVO, to the new unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: The weapons I did not receive, but if I was to go to certain duty or task, I would be given a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what duties or tasks were you assigned to while you were with the Domobran unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: While I was there I was assigned to guard the civilians in the Kaonik Prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had a house in the Kaonik village. How far is your house from the Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: About five to six hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, do you know what the purpose of the Kaonik facility was before the armed conflict which took place in the Busovaca area, that is the conflict between the Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict it was used by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time it belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the JNA pulled out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what happened to this facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: The civilians were taken there, the civilians of the Muslim ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a district military prison there or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I know it was not there, but it wasn't in this facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was in another facility, you mean another building?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, another building. Not where I guarded these civilian Muslims. It was -- that prison was in another building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. How far were these two buildings away from one another?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: About 30 to 40, maybe up to 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that as a member of the Domobran unit you were assigned to guard the Kaonik facility. What exactly was your task or duty?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: My task was that during my duty, if the prisoners, and I don't know if I can call them prisoners, but if they wanted to go to the toilet, I would open the door for them. When the food was brought to them, that I opened the door again. Sometimes they asked for wood and then I would give them wood, if it was cold. So things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you armed at that time when you guarded that building?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your relationship with these persons who were kept there who were these Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: My relationship? Everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they from? Where did they live before?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: For the most part these people were, as we called them, neighbours. They would be from neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, recall what villages?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were from the villages of Loncari and Skradno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, do you remember whether in the area of the villages of Loncari and Skradno any fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to the period of time when you were guarding the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I am talking now about the security situation during the conflict. Did shells and grenades fall around your house where you lived?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and I was wounded at that time and there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the situation was in other areas of the Busovaca municipality? Were shells falling around there as well, and was there shooting going on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: There was no location in the area where the shells did not fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it because the Defence lines or the frontlines were close by?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were very close. Busovaca is a small place, so all around there were -- are -- we called them the defence lines, and then there were the lines in between. And then there were the Muslim lines also, beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the distance as the crow flies between your house and the front lines?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: In some places it was even less than 500 metres, and in some other places up to 2.000 or 2.500.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, while you were on duty providing security at Kaonik, did you have an opportunity to be in contact with the civilians, the Muslim civilians who were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe what conditions -- what their living conditions were, where they slept, how they ate, where they went to the toilet? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I even entered the areas where they stayed. And since they were my former neighbours, I even played cards with them. May I continue now? As I said I entered there and I played cards with them. I knew a lot of them, most of them. And as far as the conditions are concerned, I know that they were not cold, they had something to cover themselves with. Whenever they asked for something, water, wood, a blanket or something, they would receive that. And we didn't -- and as far as the sleeping, we had pallets. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, do you recall personally an event, a situation where you yourself answered and provided some service to somebody who asked you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I say what it was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, I knew most of them and they knew me. I once asked Mr. Aleksovski, I told him that very frequently they wanted to go out to the toilet, and I opened the door and I let them. And I said -- I asked him if I could just let them walk around during my shift and then, at the end of my shift, they should go back into their room. And that's how it happened. And then, after a couple of days, one of them approached me because, as he said, I was good. And he said, "Ivica, could you please request of Mr. Aleksovski if I could go, I could be taken to have my haircut." So I went to Mr. Aleksovski and I -- and he said there is no problem, but just bring him back. So, since my house was near the facility, I told my wife that I would bring this man. So he came over to my place. He took a bath. I gave him a fresh change of underwear. He ate something and we went to Busovaca where he got a hair cut. We walked around Busovaca a little bit, we returned to my house, and in the evening we went back to the prison. And the man thanked me and he told me if he ever went back to his home, "here is my address, here is my phone number. Come and visit." However, I never went to visit. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this man today?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I have it written down, if you want me to I can look it up. But I forget now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it here on you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my wallet is not here. I know that his nickname was Rusmir Pasic, something like that. I know that they called him Rujo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, you said that you would enter the building where the Muslim civilians were kept, and that you played cards with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you occasionally bring something with you to share with them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I brought some alcohol with me, but I didn't do it quite on my own. I asked before I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you offered them some brandy, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. And since I am not a smoker and I was receiving cigarettes, I would distribute my cigarettes to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did you notice what food was like? What did these people eat?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: At that time the food there was kind of soldiery food. It was mostly beans and some pasta and occasionally there was meat. So I ate that food myself, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everybody ate the same food, both the soldiers and the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. They all -- everybody ate the same food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at the time, when you were on duty at Kaonik, that there was some outbreak, some disease among these people?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did you see whether these Muslim civilians, who were in this facility which you guarded, did you see them go to work, to labour?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us how this took place?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Usually somebody would come from the frontlines and would ask somebody from the military police for several, I don't know how many, people who they needed to dig some canals. Then they would come into the hangar, escorted by the military policemen, and they would take, 10, 15, however many they needed, they would take them in a vehicle and they would take them out to dig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said somebody would come. Do you mean somebody from the military?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Somebody from the frontlines. Either a commander or deputy commander. They would come to the military policemen and the military policemen would come to the hangar, and there would be a list. We had nothing with that. We had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And who would compile this list? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, tell us, if you know, whether the citizens of Croatian ethnic background, who also had this labour duty, those who were not mobilised in the HVO units who had remained back at home (sic)?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Everybody who could dig and who was not in the military was sent digging, including my uncle, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your uncle at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: He was born in 1920.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where your uncle went to perform his labour duty?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That was on the frontline at Kula and at Podjele, and a little bit at frontline at Strane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bagaric, do you know how he went to perform his labour work duty? Did somebody come to take him, did he go there on his own, how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, because we lived, one next to another, he would receive information and then he would leave there and then, when he was out, he would come back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he always receive a notice or would some soldier come to get him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would come even at night. For instance, a line would be broken and then you needed to dig a new line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of other people who had this work duty from your village, or of your neighbourhood, except for your uncle?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: As I said before, everybody who was not able to fight. There were even younger women who did not go to the frontline, but went to this work duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, you mentioned Zlatko Aleksovski. Can you tell me when you -- when it was that you met him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I met Zlatko Aleksovski when I came there to guard the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you recognise him today if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see him here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see him over there. That's the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed to the accused and identifies him as Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did you have frequent contacts with Zlatko Aleksovski or did you see him once or twice?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: While I was on duty, we saw each other. He did not give me very many orders, because I had my own commander of the Domobrans unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was Zlatko Aleksovski a member of your Domobran unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: And as far as my acquaintance with him is concerned, he took me to the health centre when I was wounded (sic).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Zlatko Aleksovski was dressed while he was at Kaonik, while you were at Kaonik? Did he wear a uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Both uniform and civilian clothes, it depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he had any insignia, any rank insignia or anything?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, tell me, at that time was it usual for the people who were not involved in the army to wear uniforms or part of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. People who received them from the HVO before, they were wearing them when they were on the frontlines, sometimes when they were at home, or when they were working, depending on the situation. It even became popular to wear some vests and t-shirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, six years have passed since. Do some people in your village still wear parts of uniforms in your village?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. A few days ago a man brought some wood to me from the forest, and he was wearing army boots and an army vest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An army vest?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that it is not unusual for civilians, at that time, and even today, to wear parts of military uniforms; is that unusual?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. At least not for us living in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice, while you were at Kaonik, in what way Zlatko Aleksovski treated the prisoners, the Muslim civilians who were there, how did he treat them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, if you were asking me whether I directly and personally saw how he treated the prisoners, I didn't. But I can tell you that he was a correct, because whenever I asked him to do something for some of the prisoners, he always said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. While you were at Kaonik, did you see any cases or incidents where somebody would beat or maltreat the Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: While I was there as a guard, I haven't seen anything like that. And what happened before that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether some of them was taken ill, seriously, or that some of them was injured or -- while you were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: While I was there, nothing like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, in the beginning of your testimony, that practically there was not a single part of the area in Busovaca which was not shelled and where the fighting was not going on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it also apply to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that was the place that was most heavily shelled but the entire area of Busovaca was shelled and not a single inch was left without shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether some of the prisoners, or the Muslims who were detained in Kaonik, were any of them wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: In Kaonik or at Busovaca, as such, I haven't heard of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you wounded, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were on duty as a guard?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how it happened?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was going to work, just as I arrived at the gate an acquaintance, or a friend and a neighbour was there, and we stopped there to talk for a while because I was early. And a shell landed four and a half metres away from me and it -- I fell down. And people who were there said that -- told Zlatko what happened. He came with the car, took me to the medical centre in Busovaca. This is where I received first aid. And from there I was transferred to Nova Bila to the hospital there. My son was later killed, accompanied me, and Zlatko drove his car back home. I don't know whether you need any more details, because my son at the time was in the military police. As soon as he heard that he (sic) was wounded, he immediately came there and his car remained when I was taken to hospital. And that is why Mr. Aleksovski drove the car home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was your son killed, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the 10th of September 1973.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, '93. He was born in 1973.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you wounded? What injuries did you sustain? Severe or light?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, the kidney now, my kidney could be seen, I have a wound which is 14 centimetres long. And I also had some slight injuries on my hands and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were lucky to stay alive?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, after you received help at the Nova Bila hospital, you were released to go home, right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: At the Nova Bila hospital I just stayed overnight, because the hospital itself was a target of shell attacks. We were told that I wouldn't be secure even there. And that is why I went to Busovaca and I remained there for some ten days, until I started -- I could walk. And that's when I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you staying at Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That was the military hospital. That's how we called it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was an outlet of the Nova Bila hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not a regular hospital before. It was used as a war hospital. It was a kindergarten before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were just beds there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was not a medical centre at Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, because it too was shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that you went home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever return to Kaonik to resume your duty there or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No not as a guard. I didn't even go to the defence lines. I went to the wood plank factory called Mediappen and I was employed there because there was some special production during war-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was another form of labour duty?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the events that you have described, did you have any connections whatsoever with the military of any kind? Were you involved in any military unit after that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was all. Do you know, Mr. Bagaric, anything about the Muslims who were at Kaonik, and you said that they were taken out for labour duty, do you know that they too were taken out for -- to be used as human shields? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that, because I wouldn't accompany them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, when they were taken out from Kaonik, these Muslims, were their hands tied up or did they go with their arms free?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, their hands were not tied up, because the car would come, they would climb and go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Were you present when they would return from the labour duty, when they were returned to Kaonik? Were you there sometimes when they returned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly no, because our shifts lasted for about two hours, and they would stay more at that digging. So somebody else would be there when they would return. Maybe I was there once or twice, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But sometimes you were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were there on a few occasions, did you notice that some of those people who would be returned, whether they were hurt, wounded or something like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. No. We even joked. They would ask me whether I had cigarettes and things like that. And they would go to take a rest. We didn't have much time for talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Bagaric, who would bring -- who had brought the Muslim civilians at Kaonik, and how did they arrive there in the first place? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not there when they were brought in, but I heard that the HVO would bring them, because they were in the -- in their zone of jurisdiction, so there was fighting there and they were behind the backs, so to say, of the defence lines, and that's why they were brought there for their own security and for our security. Because we feared because of that. And some people even liked that. I have an example where my neighbour, who returned home in the meantime, at Skradno, who said that he was -- that it was his happiest time when he was taken there, because the shells were landing and you never knew where it would hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Bagaric, whether there were some cases where those people would come of their own free will at Kaonik to feel more secure and to seek shelter from war operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I haven't seen it personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, while you were on duty, were you ever employed at the gate, at a steel gate, at the entrance to the entire complex?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I never worked there, but I was wounded there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you. Your Honours, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda Cross-examined by Mr. Meddegoda

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution sympathises with you over the loss of your son during the conflict in 1993. Having said that, I wish to ask a few questions from you on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: The witness nods and says yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, you said that after your secondary school you went to work in a company. And what was the name of that company that you worked in, after secondary school?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I have to correct myself there, because I first worked in a company, in a metal processing company, and second company which I mentioned is Pappero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the name of the metal processing company that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: The company for the processing -- for metal processing, that was the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you moved on to the Pappero company?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where you worked until you retired?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Pappero company Zenica for the professional rehabilitation of invalids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any point work in any other place, any other company?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, shortly before the war, at the mineral company outlet from Belgrade, I worked for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that company called?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Just Mineral Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever work in a company in the Vatrostalna factory?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never worked in the Vatrostalna factory?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. Only the companies that I've already listed. But during the war I worked in a Mediappen company in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a company, was it called timber?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But at that time it was not operating for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it is said that you ever did work in the Vatrostalna company, that would not be correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bagaric, you said you were first mobilised to the HVO after your retirement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was first mobilised at the HVO, but I am not retired, not even now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said you were neither retired nor employed. Yes. I remember that. And after you were mobilised, you said from there, from your mobilisation, you were transferred to the Domobran unit. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when in 1993 you were transferred to the Domobran unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime in April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was after being transferred to the Domobran unit in April of 1993 that you were assigned to the Kaonik Prison facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who transferred you to the Domobran from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: It was at my personal request, because of my poor health.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at whose instance was the transfer affected? You requested, but who ordered the transfer from the HVO to the Domobran unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I applied to my commander, and he said that he would see what he could do about it, and tomorrow he said that I should report for duty in Busovaca at the Domobrans. They are in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any written transfer order from your commander?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your commander who asked you to report the following day to the Kaonik facility in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Cosic. I can't remember his first name. And he has a brother by the name of Jago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you were injured on the day when you arrived for work in the Kaonik facility, you were injured at the gate when a shell hit you and you sustained injury?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I said it was on the 10th of June 1993. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were, upon being assigned to the Kaonik facility, you said in evidence that you had to guard the building in which the Muslim civilian -- civilian prisoners were being detained?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew most of those Muslim civilian prisoners who were detained there, as you already said in evidence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew them to be persons of -- citizens of the community who were good citizens and citizens who had not had any breaches with the law, or not any serious criminals of the area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why those Muslim prisoners were being detained in the Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I suppose that they were taken there because of their own security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Domobrans unit did not have any weapons, did it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the other guards of the Domobran unit carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you think you would have secured their safety in the case of an attack, or in the case of an invasion, when you had no weapons with you, and the Domobran unit did not have any weapons with you. Neither you nor any of the guards had any weapons with you.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: We were not sent there to try to fend off an attack, but we were sent there just to be handy, and to help those people when they need something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said a while ago they were sent there for their own safety and their own security, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. I said that they were taken there because of their own security, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have not been able to secure them in the facility without any effective weapons being given to the Domobrans unit, of which you are a member?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bagaric, you said that you know that Muslim prisoners were taken to the trenches from the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, that -- and then you said that you saw them being taken on one or two occasions. Or you saw them being returned on one or two occasions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Both. Both. I saw both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now your uncle was also a person who was taken for trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was taken from his home for trench-digging? He was not taken from a prison facility --

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was not taken from a prison facility to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: (Nod).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sought Mr. Aleksovski's permission to take a prisoner home, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I told him that this man has asked me to do him a favour. And that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, he said, "Yes, okay. But you have to bring him back in the evening."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he gave you permission to take a prisoner home and be brought back to the prison facility in the evening?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there are -- were there instances on which you -- were there other instances in which you took prisoners home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That is the case. That is the instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also, Mr. Aleksovski also gave you permission to let the prisoners out of the prison facility during the time you were on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Outside just in front of the prison building, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for that as well, I believe you asked Mr. Aleksovski for such permission?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember whether I sought that permission from Aleksovski or from somebody else who was there, military police or, I don't know how to call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you in fact -- what permission did you in fact seek from either Mr. Aleksovski or from the military police who were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, it went like this. During my two hours on duty I had at least ten interventions from civilians who were kept in that prison. They actually asked to be taken out to go to the toilet. And I had to open and close the door again, and I was -- I then asked whether I could let them out, all, because I knew that they wouldn't usurp it, but I never they had to seek permission, which was granted, to take them out while I was on duty. And when the two hours elapsed, I would bring them back. Even if they need not go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were given that permission to let them out of the prison facility and return -- and be returned to the facility during the period of your shift of guard duty?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, do you know of -- for how long -- I withdraw that question, Your Honour. Mr. Bagaric, you were in the camp from about April until the 10th of June, you were on guard duty during that entire period?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not until June. I was there since April, or from April until the beginning of May. And I was wounded because I was waiting for transfer -- to be transferred to the defence lines in Podjele as a Domobran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that -- when you were wounded, I thought you were wounded on the 10th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But at that time I was not there as a guard. I was not guarding the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your duty at that time, at the time you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of June, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, on the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after May of 19 -- so your evidence is that from April you were a member of the Domobran unit 'til May of 1993, and from May again you became a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of your duties as a member of the HVO within the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the nature of your duties as a soldier within the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I was at the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, when you were a member of the HVO, you did not perform any duties within the Kaonik Prison facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your period, did you come across a guard by the name of Zarko Petrovic within the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I did not return there any longer, any more, because there was no need for me to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Bagaric. But my question is, during the time you were there in Kaonik, that's from April to May, you remember a guard by the name of Zarko Petrovic, who was also in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. No. A guard?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A guard by the name of Zarko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody by the name of Zarko Petrovic, a guard or a member of the HVO, a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: As a guard, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: As a member of the military police did you know anybody by the name of Zarko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I heard that there was a person by that name, but I don't know what was he doing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you heard, to which unit or to which company did he belong to, Zarko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that. I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard that there was a Zarko Petrovic who was in the Kaonik Prison facility, although you do not know in what capacity he was there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I even -- I didn't even hear that he was in prison. But I know that there was a Zarko Petrovic in Busovaca, a person by that name in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew somebody by the name of Zarko Petrovic in the Kaonik Prison facility, as a guard of the Domobran unit or as a member of the HVO, the military police or any other member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: As you are saying now, no, no I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a member of the HVO by the name of Miro Maric, who was within the Kaonik facility during that time that you worked there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I know that name, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a member of the military police he was stationed at the building by the gate, by the entrance gate to the camp, was he?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Whether he was at the gate or not, I only saw him there as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he wearing at the time -- on the occasion that you saw him? What uniform was he dressed in?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: An HVO uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he carry any weapons on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I don't know. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you also recall the name of Marko Krilic, who was also in the prison facility during the time you were there, either as a guard or a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know Marko. I know him and I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Marko Krilic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: An HVO policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he wearing when he was in the camp, in the prison facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: The same clothes as any other HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also Stipo Juric, did you know a person by the name of Stipo Juric who was a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Not as a member, but I know Stipo Juric, who I believe testified here yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I am not talking of the Stipo Juric who testified yesterday who a member of the Domobrans. I am asking whether you know of a Stipo Juric who was a member of the HVO, who was in the Kaonik Prison facility at the time you were there, from April to May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Goran Medugorac, who was also in the camp, in the prison facility during the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: When I was there, there was no person by the name of Medugorac. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are sure that name doesn't ring a bell in your mind, Goran Medugorac?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I don't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also said that on occasions you used to bring alcohol to the camp facility, to the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got permission before bringing alcohol to the facility?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask for it. I did not ask for that. I would just put it in my pocket and off I go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't think it was wrong to bring alcohol to the prison facility, or illegal have brought alcohol to the prison facility without permission?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I did not think about that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did you know Mr. Aleksovski -- when did you first meet Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: When I first came to guard the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had not met Mr. Aleksovski before that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know him from the time he was in the Zenica penitentiary institution, nor did you know him at the time he was in the Vatrostalna factory?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any additional questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I have some questions for you. How many prisoners were there at the prison when you were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell exactly, because while I was there some went out digging, and how many went there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but I asked about approximate figure, 10, 100, 1.000.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: 40, 50, 60, maybe around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I did not hear the response. My interpretation was between 45 and 60.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: 40, 50, 60, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You took home only one prisoner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Why? Did you have a special relationship with him? Why did you choose this prisoner to take him home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Because he asked me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Other prisoners never requested this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. No. They did not. No one of them. They did not. No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And if all 60 prisoners requested that.

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I would have helped them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question. Did another colleague of yours also take prisoners home, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I don't think that they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You told Mr. Mikulicic that the civilian prisoners who were there for their own safety and for your safety. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What did you mean when you say your own safety? I can understand the safety of the prisoners, but when you said your own safety, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that these prisoners who were of Muslim ethnic background were behind our backs, and we shot at one another. That is, we shot at Muslims and Muslims shot back at us. And I don't think that -- and the fact that they were behind us, well, maybe they would have even signalled to them how many we were where we were. And maybe they didn't like the fact that the bullets would be flying, maybe, over us onto them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So that is why you are also saying that the civilian prisoners who were there did not -- did not need -- did not need to be guarded by weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA BAGARIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was necessary for them, and there were also not guarded with weapons. If, when we changed duties, we would give over that old rifle that we had, so then people -- I remember an old Russian automatic rifle with a drum on the top. So that's what we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bagaric. I believe that we have no further questions of you. We thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe return to your place. Thank you, Mr. Bagaric. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would like to call a fresh witness. However, we are in a similar situation as yesterday. It's 15 past one. The Defence would prefer to examine this witness continuously and we again ask the Trial Chamber for a decision on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We agree, and we would also like to point out that we only had a single break today, and I apologise for having forgotten about the second break. So maybe it is just as well that we finish a bit earlier today. Thank you very much and we will see you tomorrow.
